utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, please have the accused brought into the courtroom, the accused who is still our witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good afternoon to the interpreters in the booths. Good afternoon. Good afternoon to Defence and Prosecution counsel. Let's wait for the witness to be properly seated. Now that he is, we can say good afternoon, and now we can resume --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Good day, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: -- our work. All right. Without any further adieu, Mr. Hayman, will it be you today?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It won't be, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and to Your Honours. I wanted to raise a logistical issue with the Court. We spoke to our client after the last session on Friday a week ago, and both Mr. Nobilo and I concluded that he was totally exhausted by a week of testimony, and I think, in fact, he was exhausted by the middle of the afternoon on Friday, and that's going to cause us to go back to some of the testimony on Friday afternoon, which I don't think was as clear as it could have been. What we would like the Court to consider is shorter but more frequent breaks, so that roughly there would be 45 minutes of testimony and a short break of 10 or 15 minutes for General Blaskic to have a hot drink, relax a little bit, and then 45 minutes on, 10 or 15 minutes off, and so forth. If that could be integrated with the Court's schedule, I don't think we would lose very much time on a net basis, but it would hopefully, as the weeks cumulate, and we do think we have another three weeks probably of total testimony, both the remainder of direct and cross, something like that, we could possibly avoid a situation where the witness becomes totally exhausted and is not in a position to give his best testimony to the Court. We would ask you to consider that request. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll speak with the Office of the Prosecutor and with my colleagues, of course, whenever there is a problem of this nature, but we have to make a concrete distinction between those days when we work four days in which there are already two breaks, and then there are those sequences that go on for three hours, half days. In the half days, we take 20-minute breaks. We sometimes go a little bit longer because the Judges may be required for other responsibilities when they go back to their offices. Are you making that distinction, Mr. Hayman? How do you see that issue? Of course, I'll ask the Office of the Prosecutor for its comments, and then I'll afterwards turn to my colleagues for their advice. What do you think, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think it is an issue of cumulative fatigue from concentration and, I think, stress. There's no question it's stressful to be on trial for two years, it's stressful to be in custody for three years, and it's stressful to testify day after day. So I think it cumulates, the fatigue cumulates both on a daily and a weekly basis. So definitely at the end of a full day, there's likely to be more fatigue, and as we get towards the latter part of the week, there's likely to be more fatigue, but I don't think one can say it's simply an issue on the long days. It was interesting, in discussing this with the client, Mr. President, General Blaskic, and I don't think I'm waiving any privileges, we asked him, "What is it that you think is so fatiguing," and he said, "For three years, I've had really very little contact, personal contact, with other human beings. I haven't had a lot of conversations." He's been in court listening, but he doesn't talk. He has not been verbalising for three years, in essence. Now, certainly, he has visits and so forth, and now he's called upon to verbalise 35 or 40 hours in a very concentrated way per week for roughly six weeks, it's going to be, so that is at least part of, I think, the fatigue. He is using a part of his brain that has been, to a certain extent, put in stasis during his incarceration because of the nature of the limited contacts and limited opportunities for speech and conversation that he has, at least this was a theory that he offered. It's hard for the rest of us, quite frankly -- I'm not a scientist, I'm not a doctor -- it's hard for us to evaluate that because none of us have been put in that position, but it's of serious concern to us, and that's why we raise it and make the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll ask the accused, but before that, Mr. Kehoe, let me ask you what you think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Mr. Harmon is asking me something. I think, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Office of the Prosecutor unilaterally agrees that Your Honours are professional Judges. We simply leave it to Your Honours' discretion on this issue. I simply would encourage the witness, certainly as we have encouraged our witnesses and, Mr. President, you have in the past, that if witnesses tire at some time, that they simply ask the bench for a break. I think it might accommodate all concerns, and I leave it to Your Honours' professional judgment in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I suppose you agree with everything that was asked by your counsel, but the Judges would like to hear what you have to say. What do you feel about what was said? Do the days tire you very greatly and that you feel yourself more and more tired as the weeks go by, or as the week goes by? Would you explain that to us quickly and simply, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. President, I support everything that the lawyers said. I just wish to note one more thing: I spent two years in total isolation, that is to say, without any possibility to communicate with anyone except for my family when they would come to visit, and that is seven days per month. From the 27th of December, 1998, until you made your decision that I could go out and get some fresh air after the trial here, I practically did not spend even that one hour outdoors, and, indeed, as the end of the week approaches, I'm truly fatigued by the trial. I even fall asleep in the vehicle during that 10-minute or 15-minute ride back to the prison. Although this is city driving, it's nothing much. So if it is possible, I would appreciate it if I could testify for 45 minutes and then take a short break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'll consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we take a decision, the Judges would like to know, General Blaskic, whether, if we took a 10-minute break, you could leave the courtroom. Could you go to your place for ten minutes? If we were to grant 10 minutes, would the security services allow that? Let me turn to the registrar. I don't know how that would work. Judge Rodrigues, I think that you're familiar with these questions, if you want to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I simply wanted to know, because we can take a break, but if the break is very short, I think that you, General Blaskic, would not be able to get out of the courtroom, and I think it's very important for you to leave the courtroom for the sake of rest. I was asking Mr. Dubuisson whether, with a 10-minute pause, a 10-minute break, the General could leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. He could leave a courtroom, but it takes two or three minutes and then two or three minutes to come back. If he only had ten minutes, then he would only have five minutes outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, it would be better to take 15-minute breaks?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that would be much better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges would like to take into consideration several parameters in order to be sure that both parties have the proper position in the courtroom. For the time being, we're going to listen for one hour, that is, until 3.30, and then we will render our decision after the 3.30 break. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We shall try to communicate for the moment, so to speak, when we stopped the testimony before our one-week break. Actually, before that, I would like to ask the registrar to give you D280, the report from Ahmici, and also the three orders from the 15th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you have before you the report from Ahmici, D280, and last time, you said that it was not true, according to what you know now, in view of the events that took place in Ahmici. So can you tell me how you came to this conclusion that this was not true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. President, this report is not truthful because, in the first part, it says that the Muslim armed forces, in the early morning hours, attempted to launch an attack on the military police units located in the Bungalow. According to what I know now, on the basis of the time I spent here in the courtroom, I believe that this is not truthful because, in this report, obviously this first part is being used to justify further activities that followed in the territory of the Bungalow, Nadioci, and Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What do you mean or, rather, what do you think was falsely stated in that report that the military police was attacked? Why was it necessary to send this to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I issued two orders on the 15th of April, 1993, and in those orders, I raised the level of combat readiness, and according to the order issued at 10.00 a.m. on the 15th of April, 1993, I allowed members of the HVO to return fire conditionally, only if there was fire from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina directed at them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we get the order that you wrote on the 15th of April at 10.00 so that you would read exactly what it says, that is, D267? So could you exactly read out that part of your order?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The other side, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Have you found it? Then please read it out.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I'm reading 2.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please read it for us?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: "In case of stronger attacks, in the event of a rather strong attack by the Muslim extremist forces from the direction of the villages Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, Pirici, inform me, and if the fire is opened directly at you, return the fire and neutralise the attacker."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to this false report that the military police had been attacked, in order to justify your order, is there anything else that is missing in this report, something that you know happened, now?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The attack on civilians is missing from the reports, and the killing of civilians is missing, and the torching of buildings, houses, and other immovable property in the village of Ahmici is missing as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the report D280?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: (No audible response)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the rest of the report? I said this is D280.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The rest of the report that describes the fighting around the school, and the mosque, according to what you know now, according to what you found out during this trial, is that truthful?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said to the Court that on the 16th of April, 1993, you ordered -- you issued orders to the military police, you commanded the military police, although otherwise you did not command them especially, you did not give them combat orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the military police was attached to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please explain to the Court how this came to be, this attachment of the military police to you on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 15th of April, when I returned from the press conference, around 15.00, I talked to the head of the main staff of the HVO, and informed him about the situation, and the impressions I got after viewing the video cassette and the abduction of Zivko Totic in Zenica. I emphasised to the head of the main staff that, obviously, this is terrorism, as a form of activity of extremist forces from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina against the command cadre of the HVO. The head of the main staff agreed, and said that it was obvious that the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina would exhaust the HVO by terrorism, and then that probably an all-out attack would be launched, just as in Konjic. I also told him that in case of an all-out attack, we do not have the forces for proper defence, because the Vitez Brigade was just in the stage of its establishment of its formation. After that, the head of the main staff told me, "Well, if there were to be an all-out attack, then all forces of the military police and the PPNs would be attached to you." I asked him whether this was in order, that in case of an all-out attack, I command the military police and the special purpose units. The head of the main staff said, "Yes, that's in order. In case of an all-out attack, you will command both the military police and the PPNs."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "PPNs," what are you saying?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I'm saying "special purpose units." And he would agree on the attachment with Bruno.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who's Bruno?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Bruno was head of the defence department -- or the Minister of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, later the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the case of attachment, how many orders do we have? Who is ordering who, and who is issuing how many orders so that we would have this attachment take place, so that you would command units that were not your own?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We would always do this by way of two orders, one order that I would receive from the head of the main staff of the HVO, and another order that the commander of the unit that is being attached receives from his immediate superior, or from someone at an even higher level in military subordination. In this case, the commander of the military police was supposed to receive an order from the defence department, or perhaps from the head of the department of military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please tell the Court now, generally speaking, from what point in time did this attachment start? What was the moment when it actually started?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That is the moment when the commander from the attached unit reports to the commander to whom he is being attached, and then he puts himself at the disposal of this commander, together with his unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, generally speaking, what is this usually like in the military? What are the usual situations when there is this kind of attachment?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, these can be exercises, but it can also be combat operations. When the commander of a higher unit gives, as a reinforcement to a unit that is the protagonist of combat operations, a special unit. In order to clarify this, I'm going to give an example. For example, if an infantry battalion is there, a tank company can be attached to it in order to carry out certain assignments. The commander of the tank company, when he reports, together with his unit, to the commander of the battalion, and when he is placed at his disposal, at that moment the attachment actually starts, and the use of these forces by the commander of the infantry battalion. The order that he should report, that is to say, the commander of the tank company, he receives this from his immediate commanding officer, or from a higher officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now let us move on to Ahmici. In this specific case, what were you told? When could you use the military police?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was given an order by the head of the main staff of the HVO, that I could deem the military police attached to me if there is an all-out attack of the forces of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said to the Court that attachment starts from the moment when that unit of the military police is put at your disposal; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, on the day of the 16th of April, 1993, when did the unit of the military police put itself at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: According to my notes, at 11.45 (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you have it noted what they exactly told you? Let us recall that.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the military police reported to me, and he informed me, and I quote, "We are waging a battle. It is very tough. They are persistent, and they are firing at us with all available armaments, and even women, and the toughest -- they are the toughest in the houses around the school and the mosque."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we deem that the military police unit was attached to you at 11.42?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know when the fighting started in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Can I interrupt you for a moment, please? In the transcript, I think, 11.45 is what I see. I think that General Blaskic said 11.42.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The exact time is 11.42, so there must have been some kind of confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you know then, before 11.42, that in the village of Ahmici there was fighting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you know that in that sector, in that area, there was some kind of fighting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I did receive information that in the sector north of the road there was fighting, but exactly in the village of Ahmici, that I did not have any information on until 11.42.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At this court, did you receive information from the witnesses of the Prosecutor when the fighting actually started in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I learned about that as I listened here to the testimonies of the witnesses of the Prosecutor, and according to my recollection, it was about 5.25 or 5.30 on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that between twenty past five and 11.42, on the 16th of April, 1993, you do not know anything that happened in Ahmici; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I did not have any information as to what was going on within the village of Ahmici in that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court, according to what you heard from the Prosecution witnesses about the victims, when were all these people killed, at what time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, in the time between 5.30 and 7.00, or possibly 7.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My question then is: At the time the people, the civilians, were killed in Ahmici between 5.30 and 7.30 in the morning, was this unit attached to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You received the report D280. On the 15th of April you issued three orders, or, rather, two, relative to the military police. Could you compare what it was you ordered with what you learned from the reports, and what actually happened in Ahmici, and which you were informed about during the proceedings here? Please look at all three reports, or, rather, two which are relevant.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Could I get the two orders, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One issued at 10.00, and the other at 15.45. Let us first look at the part relative to the military police, the area of Ahmici, Santici, Nadioci and Pirici. With reference to that unit and that area, what were your orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The order issued on 10.00, point 2.1 says that I ordered that in the event of any strong attacks by extremist Muslim forces from the direction of the villages of Nadioci, Ahmici, Sivrino Selo, Pirici, I should be informed, and if the fire is opened directly, therefore, only in that case, should the fire be returned and the attacker neutralised. In this order, I have not said that the attacker should be destroyed, or that a counter-attack be launched, pursuit, or any other kind of tactical combat operation against the attacker.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: To neutralise the attacker, what kind of response is that in relation to the enemy? What does it exactly mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In any event, it is the mildest form of response, when an endeavour is made to remove the immediate danger, and that means self-defence. Of course, neutralisation may be of various degrees. Sometimes it's 25 or 50 per cent, but whether we compare it with this report --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: D280 you mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, it is obvious that my orders were overstepped, because not only was fire returned, as can be seen from the report, but combat operations were undertaken, and actions with a view to pursue and expel the attacker. The order of 10.00, I had ordered the neutralisation of the attacker, so there's no counter-attack and no pursuit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This analysis was done by comparing your order of the 15th of April, 1993, at 10.00, with the report D247, and the report from Ahmici, D280. Correction, D267 is the order, and the report is D280. If we were to compare your order with what actually happened, and which you learnt about here in court, is there any link between your order and the consequences that occurred in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No. I never ordered the killing of civilians in the village nor the torching of houses in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is the number, Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Registrar, of the document of 15 April of 15.45 hours?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D268 for the 15.45 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's D268, yes. All right. That was also addressed to the military police battalion; is that right, Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about the military police battalion which was in Ahmici, and the General is analysing his order and comparing it with the report he received and what actually happened there. That was the meaning of this. We were talking about document D267, but there is also the order D268. So the General will tell us now whether the order D268 was observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse us. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. A couple of moments ago, the General compared his order, D267, and the report from Ahmici, number D280, and the information he obtained here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you now, General, in relation to the military police, analyse your order, Exhibit 268, this is the order of the 16th of April at 15.45, and could you tell the Court what were your orders to the military police in that document?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The document D268 -- it's the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is the 15th of April. I believe the witness picked it up. The exhibit is the 15th of April and not the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The date of the order is the 15th of April, the time 15.45, and it is document D268.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In this order, 2.1 implies that combat readiness should be increased of all units, including the military police, and then in 2.3, in the zone of responsibility of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police, an anti-terrorist platoon is to be engaged in the fighting against diversionary terrorist groups of the 7th Muslim Brigade within areas of operation and location of the units. Paragraph 1 of this order, paragraph 1 indicates the location of the 7th Muslim Brigade, and the places are listed, that is, Zenica, Han Bila, Kakanj. Then my order, in 2.3, says that by speedy and resolute action diversionary terrorist groups should be destroyed and taken prisoner, that is, terrorist groups of the 7th Muslim Brigade, the accommodation facilities should be destroyed, and without excepting fighting, the unit should return to base. The focus of activities should be within the municipalities of Busovaca, Zenica, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez. The time limits and time was to be determined by the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion. Then in 2.6, I ordered that reports should be submitted to me in the evening by 18.00 hours and in the morning by 6.00 hours and any special reports as needed. Therefore, this order relates to the engagement of anti-diversionary and terrorist groups of the 7th Muslim Brigade. I did not specify the time, but I left it to the commander of the 4th Battalion to decide himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, did you mention anywhere Ahmici as a base of the terrorist groups from the 7th Muslim Brigade?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This order, was it directed exclusively to the terrorist groups of the 7th Muslim Brigade or can it, in any way, be interpreted as a command for an attack against a village?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This order focuses exclusively on diversionary terrorist groups which were part of the 7th Muslim Brigade and which were engaging in activities against the command personnel of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, these diversionary terrorist groups of this type, how strong are they usually?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They usually consist of three to five men. They are often referred to as Trojkas.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you see any link between this command and what actually happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from these orders, did you issue to the military police on the 15th of April, 1993 any other orders?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I should like to ask the registry to show the witness Exhibits D271, D272, D273, D275, and D277.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please look at these reports? They are all reports addressed to the command of the Operative Zone on the 16th of April, 1993. We will not read them because they have been admitted into evidence in the early stages of the trial. Will you please look at them and tell us whether you did receive them and read them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from these written reports and the oral reports that you testified about last time, were you informed of any other facts which would be of relevance for the reports you have discussed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any indication on the 16th of April, 1993 telling you that special attention needs to be devoted to Ahmici because something special was happening there in relation to other areas?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any indications telling you that a crime of such magnitude could occur?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, because never until then had anything like it happened in the area of Central Bosnia where I was the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell Their Honours, on the 16th of April, what did you lose, if anything? What was your score, your total score on that day in the struggle against the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, by the end of the day on the 16th of April, HVO units from Zenica at the feature Kuber were crushed, and the town of Zenica was totally blocked for any kind of movement. Within the territory of Busovaca municipality, we lost our positions at Kuber, the village of Putis, a part of the village of Jelinak, and a part of Prosje. In Vitez municipality, we also lost our positions at Kuber, the entire area of Poculica, then Grabak, north of Krcevine, trigonometric point 692, Barin Gaj, Stozerac, trigonometric point 797, the village of Sucici. In Stari Vitez, family homes belonging to the families Krizanac, Mlakic, Pavlovic, Miskovic, Mioc, Simic, Prkacin, Stojak. Croats were expelled from Grbavica. Further south at Kruscica, the BH army captured the feature Pintra, 603 trig. point, and surrounded Croatian civilians in the motels called Lovac and Ribnjak, whereas the rest were captured and taken to the elementary school. In the area of Vranjska, Croats were expelled from Zepackic and Barasin, and we lost a position, trig. point 502. At the operative level, what was most important of all was that we lost all our positions at Kuber, and the town of Vitez was totally isolated, as was my command, so that there wasn't a single road leading from Vitez towards the hospital and the logistics base at Stojkovici nor did we have a safe road that we could use towards Busovaca. The road was cut at several points or under fire control of the BH army forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, if you look at it from the military standpoint only, if you compare, at the end of the day, who had control of the key features in the Lasva River Valley, what would your assessment be? Who had the superiority on the 16th of April, which of the two conflicting armies?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina certainly gained significant operative advances, and if necessary, I can show it to you on the relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please just very briefly point out the key features for the defence of the Lasva River Valley and who had control over them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps later on the relief, we can see it exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First the map and then the model, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I'm showing Vitez, the road that leads from Vitez towards Travnik and the road that leads from Vitez to Busovaca. This is Busovaca (indicating). The army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, at the end of the 16th of April, prevailed over Kuber and the entire heights across Kuber, Vran Stijena, Kratina, Barin Gaj, Sljibcica, Tolovici, Grabak, trig. 629, and further on to Stozerac, 797, and this makes it possible to exercise control over the road from the north towards the south. More precisely, Vitez, Busovaca, this main road (indicating) was not free for traffic because the forces of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina positioned themselves at Sljibcica and Barin Gaj, and the road from Vitez towards the hospital of Nova Bila or towards Travnik was cut off physically by the BH army forces that were positioned at Grbavica and Divjak, that were practically connected with Donja Veceriska. The HVO in Vitez was isolated and prevented from any communication towards the west, towards Travnik. In Kruscica, the Croats were expelled to Motels Lovac and Ribnjak, but the position at Pintra was also taken during the course of the day by the BH army, and they controlled every approach towards Vitez and Kruscica on the main road. In Vransjka, here is 502 (indicating). Position 502 was taken, and the only thing left over was Crveno Brdce, and then there would have been a physical connection with the forces deployed at Nadioci, Vidovici, Sljibcica. So already at the end of the 16th, the HVO forces in the Lasva Valley were totally encircled and physically separated from any possibility of help to the HVO of Zenica. On the operational point of view, the army took Kuber, which is the operative base for any kind of military actions towards Busovaca, towards Vitez, or towards Travnik. That is the most important point in the area of the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us simplify this and present it from a layman's point of view. Who held the hills, and who held the valleys in that area, and what is more advantageous?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The hills were held by the BH army, and in the valleys, the HVO forces were pressed in. Of course, it's better to be on the hill, and it's a far more advantageous position, and fighting always does take place for hills. On the relief map --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just one more question. You described this siege very -- in great detail. Did you know all of this on the 16th or did you find this out during the next few days in April?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know all of this on the 16th of April. Actually, typical practice was that commanders of villages, or sectors, practically never informed about the loss of positions, but only on the recapture of positions. So very often it would happen that I would be informed that we managed to recapture certain positions, and that I had not been informed about when those positions had been lost in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that during the next break, the witness shows, with the little flags, the front line on this relief map, and then we can go back to that, because then it is going to be a position that is going to remain all the way until the Washington Accords. So that is to say, throughout this week as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Aside from the decision that we will take about breaks in general during the accused's testimony, if you're agreed, we can stop here and resume with the model. We're going to take a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is in respect of the request from the accused: Every 45 minutes we will take a 15-minute break. However, the Judges agreed that we won't work as if it were the blade of a guillotine. If there is an important explanation, the explanation will be completed, and if one has to stop before 45 minutes, we'll do that, in an intelligent way, as we ordinarily do with all our work here. There you have it, General Blaskic. You can be sure that you will be able to testify under the best conditions possible. All right. Let me get used to this new system. All right. We'll work then until 4.30. I think that there is no problem, or objection from the interpreters. All right. We can now go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, at this point we have finished with the 16th, but there is one more thing that we owe the Court, and that is: Who took what on the 16th of April? That is to say, how did that day end? Could you please show this to us on the relief map, and could you tell us which flags signify what?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. President, Your Honours, at the end of the day, on the 16th of April, the entire mountain of Kuber was under the control of the BH army, and I'm showing the front line on Vrana Stijena, and then the heights above Krtina, and north to the village of Vidovici, Sljibcica, Tolovici, Grabak, Stozerac, Grbavica, Divjak, Donja Veceriska, Gacice, Stari Vitez, Pintra, Kruscica, position 502 Vranjska, Rovna. That is the front line, and this is the region of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Theoretically, from a military operational point of view, who won and who lost the war on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is quite evident from the relief map. The most important point, Kuber, is in the hands of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and, as I already said, it makes it possible for further operations to continue, which would be logical, Nadoici, Sljibcica, until they finally took the entire road from Vitez to Busovaca, or to make an attempt to link Grbavica, Divjak, and here there was an uninterrupted communication with the forces of Donja Veceriska, and in that way to physically, totally, encircle Vitez. That is to say, that in this situation, on the evening of the 16th, the town was already encircled, without the possibility of any contact with the Nova Bila hospital, or the logistics base in Stojkovici, that is to say, with Novi Travnik and Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask the registrar to give Exhibit 284 to the witness, please. So D284, you write that during the night, between the 16th and 17th of April, at 4.00 in the morning, at dawn-break?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the heading is "Defence of Consolidated Positions." I would like to read out two sections to you, and I would like to hear your comments. First, we're going to read the third paragraph from the bottom of the page, where you are giving the following orders to the Vitez Brigade: "Use main forces to defend access roads to and from the town, especially from the direction of Poculica, and Preocica, and toward Vranjska. To achieve this, link up with police forces, and with these police forces maintain -- and with auxiliary forces maintain a blockade of the forces in the areas of Veceriska, if possible, seize Donja Veceriska; Vatrogasni Dom, the fire brigade headquarters; Kruscica; and Vranjska, with the blockade being the priority." Please tell the Court, out of these assignments that you gave to the Vitez Brigade, what can the conclusion be? What is the operative position of the Vitez Brigade in the night between the 16th and the 17th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The position was highly unfavourable, and I asked that the main forces be used to defend the access roads to the town of Vitez itself, because it was evident, from the knowledge we had, that there would be an attack that would be launched to take the town of Vitez itself, by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does this order constitute a continuity with the order issued to the Viteska Brigade on the 16th of April, at 1.30 a.m.?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, because I'm highlighting that the blockade is the priority, as well as the last defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read the last paragraph of your order from the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, 1993. "We have accomplished 80 per cent of our task today, and still need to do our utmost today. Soldiers are to be specifically cautioned about how to treat civilians." In brackets it says, "(The elderly, women and children), who are not to be killed because that is a CRIME," the last word being in capital letters. "The Commander Colonel Tihomir Blaskic," at 4.00 in the morning. Why did you write that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was obvious that the brigade hadn't been established yet, and that, actually, there was disarray. I tried to encourage them to succeed in the defence of the villages and the areas that remained under HVO control. Although the situation was unfavourable, and apart from all of Poculica, from which about 460 civilians had been expelled then, and the civilians of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Grbavica, in these other areas we managed to hold on even with these forces, and, therefore, I encouraged them to persevere in these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "We have accomplished 80 per cent of our task," 80 per cent of what? What was the task of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The task of the Viteska Brigade was to defend the access roads to the town and also, as a priority, to carry out a blockade, a blockade of Vranjska, Kruscica, and the other areas, and this can be seen from this point of paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page, those are the tasks for the next day, the 17th, but then when you are summarising here, when you say "We have accomplished 80 per cent of our task," then that is what happened on the 16th, and what was the task of the Viteska Brigade on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was the blockade of Kruscica, Vranjska, and Donja Veceriska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that in keeping with the orders that you issued, D267?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The order issued at 1.30, I don't know the exact number, so if that's it, then yes, that is in keeping with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At 1.30 is 269. So this assessment, "80 per cent of our task," is that in line with the orders you issued on the 16th of April at 1.30?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to the other part of the sentence. You are cautioning soldiers as to how they should treat civilians, and you say that they should not be killed because that is a crime. What motivated you to put that in your first order after the end of the first day of war in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The first day was when a meeting was held through the mediation of UNPROFOR between the representatives of the Operative Zone and the representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Nova Bila, in Vitez, and when returning from these discussions, Marko Prskalo informed me that, during the ride, he saw killed civilians just by the road from the UN base to the Hotel Vitez, and I wanted to state it to all military conscripts that violence against civilians is a crime, and I wanted to caution them preventively that they should particularly take care of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You say that you preventively cautioned them, but did you know that a great crime had already been committed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell us, according to the reports that you received, the fighting took place in Vitez and in other inhabited areas. This type of battle, does it speak of a difficult situation for civilians in terms of military theory?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is certain that fighting in inhabited areas is very complex, when civilians can get hurt, and during such fighting in inhabited areas, it is very difficult to foresee operations, destruction, and casualties on the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: For a moment, we're going to leave aside this first order of yours, and could you please tell the Court now -- I imagine you went to sleep sometime around 4.00 in the morning -- what the next day was like? So could you tell us about this on the basis of your own notes and on the basis of your own recollection without my intervention? Please tell us about this.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 6.15 on the 17th of April, 1993, I was called up from the Vitez Brigade and asked for a particular kind of ammunition, that is, 20-millimetre and 40-millimetre ammunition. We checked to see whether we had such ammunition in stock or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I said I wouldn't intervene, but I have to. Regarding the previous order that we discussed, and if you wrote that order at 4.00 a.m., and you have a contact with the Vitez Brigade at 6.15, does that mean that you slept roughly two hours?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That night, there was no time to sleep. I was in the basement of the hotel. If I slept, I may have dozed off at one of the three tables that we had there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 6.35, we sent information to the Viteska Brigade, the mixed artillery battalion, the number was 01-4-295/93, and another information to the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, the number was 01-4-296/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993. I cannot recall at this point the contents of that information. At 6.40, I called up the commander of the 111th Brigade in Zepce, Mr. Ivo Lozancic, but the officer on duty answered the phone, and I warned him that, in the course of the day, he would be receiving a document and that it was important for the commander, Lozancic, to study it and to call me up in person after doing so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours what the plan was for Zepce?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In view of the extremely unfavourable situation for Vitez, when our very survival there was in question, I had intended to caution Zepce, Novi Sehir, and Usora and to stage demonstrative operations and to arrange them by phone so as to resist the pressure coming from Zenica towards Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "demonstrative attacks," what are they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: False attacks. They begin and end with telephone calls and an open conversation, so that we hoped that the intelligence service of the 3rd Corps would probably be able to register those conversations and would react to them, to those conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The translation is not correct. What kind of attack did you mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I said "false attack."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: About 6.40, we received a report from the Viteska Brigade, the number was 02-125-16/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993 at 06.00. At 06.50, I spoke to the main headquarters of the HVO in Mostar, and I informed them of the movement of strong forces from the direction of Zenica in the direction of Vitez and Busovaca and the obvious regrouping in the region of Kuber and Saracevica. At 6.53, I spoke to the commander of the artillery, and I asked for a summary report about the tasks accomplished from the previous day. At 6.55, I was called up from Fojnica, and we exchanged information about developments and the situation. At 7.00 -- rather, 7.06, I also spoke to the Travnik Brigade, and again we exchanged information on the situation, and before that, I had sent a warning to the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade not to issue orders on the open telephone line. At 7.16, Commander Lozancic called me up from Zepce, and I repeated to him the instruction that when he receives an order, he should study it and inform me whether he understands it. This was the order for false attacks. At 7.18, such an order was issued, the number was 01-4-298/93, dated 17th of April, 1993 at 6.45, and this order was addressed to Zepce, and the content is a false attack of Zenica. At 7.20, the deputy commander of the civilian police station in Vitez called, and he informed me that snipers belonging to the BH army were firing from Stari Vitez towards Kamenjaca, a Croatian village, and that a firing position had been identified in Polje, the second house with three stories, and from the middle level, from the first floor, M-34, and left and right of it were sniper positions. At 7.35, I had a talk with the town mayor, Mr. Santic, who asked, "Who was the organiser of the meeting at 9.00 on the 17th of April between representatives of the HVO and the BH army in Vitez?" We told him that the meeting had been organised by the British Battalion of the UN and that it would be held in the UN base. Mayor Santic also called the chief of staff, Franjo Nakic, but we told him that Nakic was absent and that he was at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why was Nakic at home? Could you explain that to the Court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Franjo Nakic, the chief of staff, was blocked in his village of Zabilje. He was blocked by forces of the BH army, and he could not reach the Vitez Hotel, but he did call up by phone, and on the 15th, at his own request, for reasons of health, he asked to be allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 7.38, I requested the commander of the Fojnica HVO battalion to report to me following order number 01-4-297/93, dated 17th of April, 1993, at 7.30. At 7.50, I received a report from the commander of the Viteska Brigade, and I gave him instructions regarding further action. At 7.55, command officer of the Operative Zone called, Mr. Dragan Kopcalija, and he informed us that he could not arrive to the Hotel Vitez as he was supposed to do, because he had been blocked by the BH army. At 8.00, with the artillery commander, I corrected the firing positions. At 8.02, I spoke to the commander of the 1st Battalion from Zenica, and he inquired about the situation, and informed me that he was at the Gudelji positions. At 8.06, a protest was issued, because of the offensive actions by the BH army, to the European Monitoring Mission to the United Nations, and representatives of the European Community, and the number of that process is 08-4-299/93, dated 17th of April, 1993, at 7.45. At 8.15, a public announcement was issued. The number was 08-4-300/93, dated 17th of April, 1993, at 8.00. At 8.17, I had a conversation with Mr. Dario Kordic, and I informed him that attacks by the BH army had started at 5.25, from the region of Grablje, and Dvor against Gavrine Kuce, and Jelinak. Then I also informed him on the casualties, 15 dead, and that during the day a meeting would be held at 9.00, between representatives of the HVO Operative Zone, and the BH army, and the UNPROFOR base, and that the subject to be discussed was a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: These 15 dead that you informed Mr. Kordic about, who were they? On whose side were the casualties?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On the HVO side. Those were the figures that I had at that point in time, on the basis of the reports I had received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 8.30, a typist from the headquarters of the Operative Zone called up to say that she couldn't come to work because of the operations and the blockade. The 8.40, we received information from the Military Intelligence Service, warning us of these open conversations between the Vitez and the Travnik Brigades, and at 8.50, I addressed a written report to the chief of staff of the main staff of the HVO regarding the current situation, and the number of that report is 01-4-302/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993, at 8.00. At 9.00, Mr. Prskalo, Marko Prskalo, and Zoran Pilicic, officers of the Operative Zone command, and my assistants, went to the meeting at the UN base, and they were transported there by officers and soldiers of UNPROFOR, and taken to the Nova Bila base. The meeting was with representatives of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the aim of the meeting, the purpose of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The meeting had been scheduled already on the 16th of April, 1993, and the aim was a cessation of hostilities, and improvement of the situation, and a general cease-fire. At 9.40 (sic), I received a call from Commander Cerkez requesting assistance and support from artillery against targets 836 and 894 (sic). At 9.17, I spoke to the deputy commander, Vinko Baresic, in Zenica, and I inquired about the situation in Kuber, and I asked him to re-establish the link between the members of the HVO in Zenica and the members of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we go back to 836 and 897, the targets? Are you aware which positions they were?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say just now what positions they were, but probably we already had a plan of artillery fire at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Talking to the commander of the HVO brigade in Zenica, I said that Mount Kuber was of extreme importance, and that he should try to keep control of it at all costs, at least of the slopes of Kuber, because our very existence would be called in question if we were to completely lose Kuber, lose control of Kuber. At 9.21, I spoke to commander Lozancic in Zepce, and required that he proceed as ordered, and that he direct his forces according to orders received, and that his main forces should be mobile and ready for movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you talking about the false order for an attack on Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I spoke on the phone, and these were the words I openly used on the telephone when speaking to Ivo Lozancic. At 9.22, I addressed a warning to the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, cautioning him that he should implement orders received from me, to the letter, and that he should supply me with precise, accurate, and timely reports regarding the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, is it customary for the commander to ask a subordinate to be accurate in his reports, and to specifically require that his orders be carried out? Why did you ask that, and why was this recorded?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is not customary, but it was almost a regular occurrence. I have already said that commanders, as a rule, would not issue precise reports, and this was a hindrance to us in our ordering, and command, and control, and I did everything to learn, in detail, what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 9.25, I spoke to the main staff of the HVO, and I informed them that attacks by BH army forces, from the direction of Zenica, were being intensified, that throughout the front line there was evidence of regrouping, and that the whole front line was active. I briefed the main staff of the fact that I had sent an order to the commander in Zepce, in accordance with permission received from Brigadier Petkovic, and this was a false attack, and I asked the main staff for information about the situation in Jablanica and Konjic. I checked whether it was true that Konjic had fallen, and that the Croats had been driven out of Konjic, or, rather, that the HVO had been driven out of Konjic. I received the answer that that was not true, and I also said that the main staff should inform the public that we were under attack by about 1.500 Mujahedeen, that is, members of the 7th Muslim Brigade. At 9.30, Pero Skopljak called up, and learned about the exchange of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Pero Skopljak was a civilian official at the time; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a civilian official at the time. At 9.40, I provided instructions for the drafting of an order, number 01-4-303/93, dated 17th of April, 1993, at 9.10. This was preparation and linking of forces which were attacking the HVO. The purpose was to relieve pressure of the Vitez and the Busovaca front lines. At 9.45, I requested a contact with the commander of the military police, Pasko or Vlado. They told me that he was not available, and I left a message saying that when they come, they should call me up, on the phone. At 9.50, the commander of the Vitez Brigade asked for assistance in personnel, for the purpose of defence from attack coming from Sljibcica. The attacks were being carried out by the BH army. At 9.52, I called up the commander of the artillery battalion, and gave him the target, elevation point 592, which he was supposed to gain control of. Officer Vlado Juric called up from the artillery, and informed me that firing would start in 10 to 15 minutes, against target 592. He required surveillance in order to correct the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember this elevation point? Was that Sljibcica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was the dominant feature from which one has control of the main Vitez to Busovaca road.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 10.05, Mr. Slavko Marin spoke to the commander of the artillery, and reminded him that we had requested elevation point 592, but that we insist that only the artillery commander should respond to our telephone calls, in order to have accuracy of reports and orders for fire. At 10.25, we again spoke to Commander Cerkez, that is, Slavko Marin spoke to him, and he asked that Cerkez report to us the positions with precision from which the BH army was staging an artillery attack against the Vitez HVO. Cerkez reported that it was either Preocica or Bukve. At 10.30, the intelligence officer asked me for permission to go towards Mahala to record the combat operations between the HVO and the BH army in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you use the word "Mahala," you mean Stari Vitez, which was under the control of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At 10.32, I was called up by the artillery commander who informed me that he had fired towards Sljibcica and that he would be ready to fire towards Kuber. At 10.45, I required from the artillery commander that he should fire at targets in the direction of the villages of Merdani and Gumanci, 500 metres to the south. At 10.46, there was a call from the commander of the Travnik Brigade to whom we conveyed the message that Zdravko Lovrenovic would remain chief of staff of the Travnik Brigade, and the commander of the Travnik Brigade confirmed receipt of that message. At 11.00 hours, I spoke to the artillery commander to check whether he was ready to fire and requiring from him that he expedite preparations for action.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, the 45 minutes has expired, so I propose a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course. All right. We will have to try to adapt things to the circumstances. Let's take a 20-minute break, and when we resume at a quarter to five, we will be able to continue until a quarter to six.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, we stopped somewhere around 11.00, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed and tell us how the events unravelled from there.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.02, we called the commander of the Viteska Brigade, and we sought information as to who was firing, and the answer was that the firing came from the HVO. The firing was in the immediate vicinity of the hotel, so we didn't know what all this was about, whether it was artillery fire against the hotel or whether it was HVO soldiers that were opening fire. At 11.10, the commander of the Viteska Brigade called Slavko Marin and gave him the coordinates for the Samar target and for the Kuber target. Both targets are to the north of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was at the targets of Samar and Kuber? What was there?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the target of Samar was the artillery of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and at Kuber also, there were military and artillery formations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including at one part, at the west of Kuber, tank positions as well of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Please proceed. By the way, did you have any tanks at that time in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, not at that time and not ever, until the Washington Accords, did we have a tank in the HVO in Central Bosnia in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.12, I called the commander of the artillery, and I sought information as to whether he was preparing to fire against these targets, and I asked for target 915, to fire one artillery piece against that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On several occasions, you mentioned targets that are marked either "915" or any other number.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Last time, you said that on the 16th of April, on the first day of the war, you did not have a plan of artillery fire against the Muslims. Could you tell us, when did you make this plan of artillery fire, and what did you mark with these numbers that were the targets?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The plan of artillery fire, I do not recall exactly, but it must have been the 17th of April, during the course of the morning, that we had already made it, and these numbers depict military positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were already observed on the 16th of April during combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Today, do you recall what target this number exactly meant?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But do you remember the principle that was your guiding principle when you were making this plan of artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That, I do recall. These were exclusively military positions and military targets of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever in your military career set a civilian target as a target for artillery fire?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed with the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.12, we also received information that UNPROFOR armoured vehicles were in the village of Preocica. At 11.14, the assistant for IPD returned. He did not manage to go towards Mahala because there was heavy sniper fire from Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "IPD," what service is that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That is "Information Propaganda Service," that is to say, information service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is that something different from military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is quite different from military intelligence, and it has nothing to do with military intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this officer inform you where the fire was coming from and why he couldn't get out of the hotel?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he could not get out because of sniper fire by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from the group of houses above the bus station of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed with the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.18, I talked to the commander of MTD, that is to say, of the artillery once again, and I asked him to speed up preparations, and he informed me that he had certain difficulties and that he would let me know when he was ready. We also sent a protest because of the sniper operations of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, number 08-4-304/93, from the 17th of April, to the European Monitoring Mission and the International Red Cross. At 11.20, I received information from the Military Intelligence Service in which they informed me that the wounded soldiers of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina were changing into civilian clothes and then using UN vehicles in order to be transported to the hospital. He also sent me information as follows: If HVO soldiers had to retreat from Kuber, they should destroy buildings for shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What kind of buildings are these?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These are mainly shelters, trenches, small buildings, military buildings that are built for protecting men and in order to make it possible for them to stay at combat positions, and also they can easily be altered and used by the party that was taking them over. This side, the BH army could take over these pillboxes and use them for their own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All right. Would you please continue?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.22, I sent an order, number 01-4-305/93, from the 17th of April, 1993, at 11.10 to the commander of the Zenica Brigade of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know now recall the content of this order?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall the content of the order now, but in my notes, I have the number of that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have a bit of a problem. I'd like to ask something of Mr. Nobilo and of the witness. When you say, "These are my notes," General Blaskic, you say, "I don't remember the contents of the order, but I noted 01-04/" and the various numbers. I don't think this was tendered. I could speak of other orders at this time as well, but the witness said, "I gave this order." Therefore, now I want to speak directly to the witness. You've got a good memory because you say "At 11.20, 11.21, 11.22," et cetera. So you took 04-4 -- you had the time to take all of those numbers down, "01," et cetera. How many telephone lines did you have, first of all? There was one point I wanted to ask you that. I don't know whether Mr. Nobilo can answer it or you, but how many telephone lines did you have? I have the impression that you spent your time moving from one telephone to another telephone, and I realise that this was the war, but was it the people who worked with you? Was it yourself? I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there was a total of two telephones, and you're right, they were practically online all the time, and there were very many orders, and what I have noted is the original number of the order, but I cannot recall the content of that order. If I were to see it, it would probably refresh my memory, and would I probably remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but we have to realise that what's important today for us, of course, is the number of the order. Since we're not going to see the order, we don't know. You have to remember what the contents were, so that the Prosecutor can also do his work, because you had the time to write 01-4-305/93. That's very good. That's excellent that you were able to do that in the midst of battle, you were able to take notes like that. I could ask Mr. Nobilo the question, because I don't want to worry you, this is part of your testimony, I realise that, but how could that be, Mr. Nobilo, you who have an answer for everything ordinarily. Could you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Of course, I wasn't there in 1993, but I learned from the witness. I can tell you very briefly, but I think it's better for the witness to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, first of all, tell me, General, in the middle of the war, as the President of our Trial Chamber has asked, how did this happen that somebody would be noting exactly what was happening? How did you do this? Who did this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the 16th of April, in the morning, as I arrived in the basement of the hotel, I told one of the men there, his name was Ljubo Jurcic, I said, "Write down everything you hear, and everything that happens here, every word I say, every contact Slavko Marin and I have via telephone, and write down the contents and the time of these events."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And what about Jurcic? Did he do anything else during those two or three days of war, except write down this diary?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: He didn't do anything else, except for this diary. He's not a military man anyway. He is not a professional from the military, so that he could be engaged for any other job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I think this is the right time. General Blaskic, you gave that order to the NTC. What was the reason for it? What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wanted to have some kind of testimony, some kind of record about everything that happened, and everything I did, and everything that my associates did, on the 16th, and on all these other days, in terms of these activities that were ongoing, so that we would know precisely what the time was when things happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You said that already, but didn't you have some type of a log of some kind? Perhaps you would have needed that person for the war.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood the question correctly, I mean, in terms of this record-keeping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question was to know whether or not -- wouldn't it have been easier to have had a recording of it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Now I understand. Now I understand the question. I'm going to explain it to you now, although -- Your Honour, on the 16th, in the morning, we went down into the disco club of that hotel. There was a disco club in the hotel, that was open late into the night between the 15th and the 16th. We had three desks. There were seven of us, and three candles, at the beginning, and out of the seven men there, as far as I can remember, I did my best to involve everyone in some kind of particular work. Ljubo Jurcic had only completed a higher administrative school, and he wasn't even a regular student. He didn't really have any military knowledge, except that he was a soldier, I imagine. I wanted to have some kind of diary. Of course, a cassette recording would have been better, but we had two telephones, and three candles at the very beginning, and that is how we worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, let me follow up the question which my colleague asked you, with this little question: At the time, you, doubtless, thought that you would need, at some later time, to make some use of the record which you had asked to be prepared. At the time, what kind of use did you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In terms of the education I received in the former army, whenever there is an exercise going on, or any kind of military activity, always there is some kind of log of operations, of things that are going on. Sometimes in wartime, this is called a war diary too. Then in a very abbreviated form, certain activities are recorded, and the time is specified very precisely. I wanted this kind of a diary to exist, and to have some kind of document remain. I thought that any document was better than no document whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Apart from the events which occurred on or around 16th April, there were other events which involved military clashes. Did you have a similar record prepared of all the activities of which you were aware in respect of those other clashes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: From the month of April, for example, and then practically until the Washington Accords, to the best of my recollection, there was an operational logbook. I'm not sure if it was called operational logbook, or whether it was called the war diary, or the logbook of the officer on duty, or whatever, but there was some kind of record that was kept throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards this document of Mr. Ljubo Jurcic, did he give it to you at one point? Did he give it to your Defence counsel? You don't have to answer if you don't want to, but did you have it, because you were so specific when you say that I -- well, sometimes one wonders if you even had the time to get an answer on the telephone. You said you made a telephone call at 11.20, then 11.21. I'm not very good at telephoning, but it seems to me that even if I call my secretary by phone, I wouldn't be able to make three phone calls in one minute, but, of course, I'm not in a war. My question is, Mr. Blaskic, it's important, I say it somewhat jokingly, but here you're giving us your version of the facts, and you're saying that, "I gave the order, number 01-4-493." You're the only one who can say whether you gave that order or not. Let me go back to the military log. Was it given to you at some point? What it given to the Defence? If you don't want to answer, don't, it doesn't matter to me, but if you want to, that would throw some light on what we're doing. But is it your memory on which you're relying in order to say that, "I called at 11.00," for example? Do what you like. Your counsel prefers that you not answer, there's no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, he's already explained that. It was before the break of last week. So we certainly have no objection to him explaining it again, and perhaps in the translation it didn't come across clearly, but we would ask that he do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But as regards the military log of Mr. Ljubo Jurcic, I don't think that an answer was ever given to a question, because I never -- I myself never asked the question, nor did my colleagues, I believe, a question about what happened to Ljubo Jurcic. Is he still alive? Does he still have his military log? Did he give it to you? How do you use it? I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, our witness will be very happy to answer your question, where this document is, when he last saw it, and how it happened that he has all these data laid out so very precisely, and that he's now in a position answer all your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You don't have to answer right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I can answer, Your Honour, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, when I found out about the indictment, I was still head of the main staff of the HVO, and during November and December, or, rather, the end of November and beginning of December, 1995, I tried to get a hold of all the important documents, and I literally copied some of these documents as I was preparing my notes for my encounter here, for my testimony, and for my trial. What I'm testifying to here now is not the war diary of Ljubo Jurcic, but allow me to explain this. Ljubo Jurcic was an officer in the command of the Operative Zone, and this is part of that operative diary which Ljubo Jurcic, as an officer, only wrote then. So this is the contents of the logbook of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia at the time when I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In order to clarify this, because my colleague tells me it is not quite clear in English, is there one diary or two diaries? Is there one that is owned by the Operative Zone, or was it Ljubo Jurcic who only took these notes? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
