utterances.text: Yes, there is only one diary, which was then written by Ljubo Jurcic, but that is the operative logbook of the command of the Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this that you are using now, is that the operative logbook, or are these your own personal notes you made while you were still in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and while you were preparing to go to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: These are my notes that I copied out of this operative logbook, which, at the time when I was the head of the main staff of the HVO, was accessible to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, so that I understand all of this clearly, I'd like to ask you another question. I remember that when you assumed your duties in Gornji Vakuf, you received a diary, a log, but in my mind, it seems to me that there was nothing in the log, the names of the commanders were not in it. However, when you speak about the journal today, or the log today, it's very detailed, and as you said, you chose something that was important from your perspective. Are we speaking about the same diary, that is, the diary that you received in Gornji Vakuf when you took your command responsibilities, or something else, another one?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, what you said is true. In Gornji Vakuf I did receive a war diary, and it is different from the operative log, as follows: According to the way I was trained and educated, and the way in which we worked, in the operative log the precise timing for every document is given, and the time of issuance is stated, whereas the war diary, the way we kept it in Gornji Vakuf and in Vitez, contained, for example, information that on such and such a date a meeting was held, and sometimes the participants of the meeting were mentioned there, and sometimes even the entire discussion. Actually, this was information as to what happened during the course of one day, but it wasn't that rich in content in terms of actual events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would like to continue along the same line of your questioning. Keeping an operative log, is that a routine matter for all trained officers?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to the JNA doctrine, according to which you did your military education, is every unit supposed to have this kind of a log or a similar log?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: If we are talking about peacetime conditions, then already from the level of battalion, there is an operative log that is kept by the duty officer in that battalion. If we're talking about conditions of war, then from the level of commander of the battalion in the former JNA, that's the way it was, a war diary is kept as a combat document, and also there is an operative log, but the lowest rank in the former JNA was that of battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Are these documents in the archives? You still had official responsibilities. Are they in the official archives? I suppose they are. The ones who had them didn't really keep them; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court when and where you last saw them.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, when I was chief of the main staff, these diaries and logs were in the archives, that is to say, November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just to clarify matters further, are these documents official documents that commanders must keep?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, and there's also a prescribed way in which they should be kept and also a time limit until when they should be kept, some for ten years, and also where they are to be kept, either in the central archives, or in the archives of the main staff, or the command that actually kept this log, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we conclude that this was not your private affair or a question of your own will, whether you were supposed to do this, but according to military doctrine, you were supposed to keep this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is the duty of every commander in war, from battalion commander upwards. It is his duty and obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thanks to your observance of military obligations, we continue now with the 17th of April, 1993 at about 11.22.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.22, we had stopped with the order that I have already mentioned that was addressed to Zenica, to the Zenica HVO Brigade. At 11.26, I had a talk with Mr. Dario Kordic who inquired about the situation and developments in the Lasva River Valley. At 11.29, the commander of the 312th Mountain Brigade of the BH army in Travnik called me up, the name is Mr. Ahmed Kulenovic, and he asked me to assist and protect his family who were living in Divjak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you tell us, where is Divjak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Divjak is in Vitez municipality. I assigned officer Zvonko Vukovic the task to take care and protect this family. At 11.35 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One further question: Ahmed Kulenovic, is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Muslim Bosniak, the commander of the 312th Mountain Brigade of the BH army in Travnik at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 11.35, the artillery commander called and informed me that he had fired a missile, and I asked him to prepare fire for the next target. I also asked surveillance of targets by the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade. At 12.00, I again talked to the commander of the MTD who informed me that firing had not been carried out, but that it would be shortly. At 12.02, we received a report from the head of the intelligence service telling us that the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina were linking up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How does the Military Intelligence Service learn about these things?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In most cases, it was by intercepting conversations on the open line, probably between commanders of lower units of the 3rd Corps of the BH army but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But which medium was used?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: An open radio link. Also all reports and information that would reach them were used by the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 12.05, I sent my response to a query, the response had the number 01-4-308/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993, issued at 11.35 and addressed to the HVO Zenica Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember the contents of your response and the query?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I do not remember the content of the question nor the response.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 12.05, we were informed that Mr. Marko Prskalo and Mr. Zoran Pilicic, officers of the Operative Zone command, had been wounded in front of the main entrance to the Vitez Hotel and that they were being given first aid in the hall of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, these officers who were wounded in front of the Vitez Hotel, who wounded them and where were they coming from? Could you give us more details about that event?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The officers were returning from a joint meeting which had been organised with UN mediation between the HVO and the BH army at the UN base in Nova Bila. They got off at the petrol station in front of the main entrance to the Vitez Hotel where they had been brought in an armoured vehicle by UNPROFOR. When they tried to cross the open space to reach the Vitez Hotel, accompanied by a communications officer from the UNPROFOR command in Nova Bila and by another person who was the interpreter, sniper fire was opened at them by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a moment. There's a mistake in the translation. You said "a UN communications officer"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It should be a liaison officer, that's what I meant, a UN liaison officer, who was escorting and protecting the two negotiators, Marko Prskalo and Zoran Pilicic, and BH snipers from Stari Vitez opened fire at them and wounded the two officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: They were parliamentarians, negotiators on your behalf. You had sent them to this meeting with the BH.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were just returning from that meeting. The meeting had ended only some 10 or 15 minutes before that. They were negotiators on behalf of the command of the Operative Zone with the representatives of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 12.07, I had another talk with the artillery commander requiring him to repeat operations, and later, at about 12.10, I talked to Zoran Pilicic, who was slightly wounded, and he came to the basement and informed me about the negotiations and the agreement reached at those negotiations with representatives of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell us briefly, as far as you can remember, what was the agreement reached with the BH army? What did your negotiator tell you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Zoran, at the time, was under stress, but he had taken note of the points of the agreement, and I have them in the way that they were conveyed to me at 12.10 on the 17th of April: A cessation of fire had been agreed, then an exchange of all prisoners, the withdrawal of forces, the positioning of UNPROFOR armoured vehicles in town at the flash points, and the formation of a joint commission for joint investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us whether representatives of UNPROFOR or, rather, the United Nations participated in those talks?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The meeting was chaired, as far as Zoran informed me, at first by Major Waters and later by Colonel Stewart, and they were the mediators, and they participated in the drafting of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At the time, how did you understand the link between a cease-fire and the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: My understanding was based on the information that I had both from the International Red Cross, and I knew that their position was that the release of prisoners should be preceded by a cease-fire and the assurance of safety and security for the release of prisoners, and virtually all agreements contained this provision and this sequence of events, a cease-fire and the removal of the consequences of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is your opinion that a cease-fire has to precede the release of prisoners or can it take place simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It is very important that a cease-fire must precede the release of prisoners by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 16th of April, did you order any arrests?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What would it have actually meant if you had unilaterally released all the prisoners when you learnt about them without previously having achieved a cease-fire? What would that have meant in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: They would have been exposed to killings, and I would be acting contrary to the position of the International Red Cross because their position always was, and I think it was a positive attitude, that safety had to be ensured first before prisoners could be released. Without safety, it would mean exposing people to the threat of being killed as a result of combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Linked to these wounding incidents, you took certain measures. You protested. I'm referring to the wounding of your parliamentarians.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Already at 12.15, we addressed a request to UNPROFOR asking them to come and transport the two wounded officers to the hospital because we didn't have any road open to us which we could use to do it ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "we," let us make it quite clear: Did you personally call them or one of your officers?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember that because, in my notes, it just says "a call to the UN"

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 12.17, a protest was drafted, the number being 01-4-307/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993, and it was addressed to the monitoring commission, the UN, the European Union, and the commander of the 3rd Corps. At 12.23, a warning was drafted, the number being 08-4-309/93, dated the 17th of April, 1993, and addressed to all assistants for information activities, IPD. I personally spoke to the artillery commander, trying to verify why there were no reports from them for a whole hour and why they still had not carried out the requested firing. At 12.28, I spoke to the commander of the police station, the civilian police station in Vitez, Mr. Samija, and inquired about the security situation in the town of Vitez. At 12.28, the head of the HOS (sic) sent a report saying that --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There's a mistake in the translation. You said "head of VOS," rather than "HOS." What does VOS mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Military Intelligence Service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the head of the Military Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the time, it was Ivica Zejko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it's the same Ivica Zejko who testified here?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed. What did Ivica Zejko inform you about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Ivica Zejko reported that the obvious intention of the BH army forces in Donja Veceriska was to link up with the BH army forces at Grbavica via Divjak. However, for the moment, the forces of Bosnia-Herzegovina army, in Donja Veceriska, were short of ammunition, and they had requested assistance from the United Nations in the form of ammunition, supplying them with ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR promise to supply the ammunition?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Sejko reported that UNPROFOR had promised to supply them with the requested ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, how did Sejko learn about this, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I assume, again, that this was a recorded conversation between the command in Donja Veceriska and the command of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You assume that this conversation was by radio link?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At 12.32, the commander of the mixed artillery battalion informed me that firing had been carried out, and he required surveillance for the purpose of making any corrections. I called UNPROFOR again, asking them to come and transport the wounded officers, emphasising that if in the case that they do not have an ambulance, they could come with a transporter, an armoured transporter, because Prskalo urgently needed aid, as he had been seriously wounded. At 12.35, Slavko Marin spoke to an United Nations officer, on the same subject, the transportation of the wounded officers. At 12.37, I again spoke to the artillery commander, who informed me that he would be ready to fire very shortly. At 12.38, Slavko Marin called the commander of the air defences, and asked for a report regarding the artillery pieces, their deployment, and their functioning order. At 12.39, the artillery commander informed me that he had fired at the target, as requested. At 12.50, I asked for a report from the commander of the military police, and the commander of the HVO brigades in Zenica, Vitez, and Travnik. At 12.57, there was another conversation with the artillery commander, who was asked to fire, upon making corrections. At 12.59, a written request was issued. The number is 01-4-311/93, dated 17 April, 1993. It was a request for provision of information on the situation, and the request was addressed to the following brigades: The Viteska, Novi Travnik, Kiseljak, Zenica, Busovaca, Travnik, Frankopan Brigades, and the artillery command, the command of the air defences, and of the 4th Military Police Battalion. At 13.01, I spoke to the artillery commander, and corrected the firing range, and asked that he repeat the firing from one artillery piece. At 13.04, a request was again addressed to the artillery, by Slavko Marin, to prepare to fire at the target at Samar. At 13.07, we checked with the artillery, whether this fire had been carried out. At 13.10, a reply was sent to the Travnik Brigade, the number was 01-4-312/93, dated 17 April, 1993, and the content of the document was a request for the issuance of artillery. At 13.13, I personally spoke again to the artillery commander, to check whether fire had been carried out as requested. He informed me that it had not been carried out yet. At 13.14, Mr. Dario Kordic called me, inquiring who was operating on Busovaca. I answered that according to the information available to us, the fire was coming from the BH army. At 13.17, Mario Cerkez called Marin Slavko, my associate, and asked for assistance for Novaci. That is a village on the main road from Vitez to Travnik, where, as we learned later, the front line had been broken through. At 13.20, a protest was addressed to UNPROFOR. The number was 01-4-310, dated 17 April, 1993. I was informed by the artillery that firing had been carried out, and they asked us to check so as to be able to make corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember or not the contents of this protest?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I know that one of the protests was addressed to them because of the wounding of the officers Prskalo and Pilicic, but I'm not sure that that is this particular protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 13.24, I called the artillery commander again, and asked him to prepare for fire at the next target. The number of the target was 1, and the artillery commander required some time to prepare to fire. At 13.30, I was called up by Mario Cerkez, who informed me about the situation in Novaci, and I cautioned him, "Not against civilians," meaning that the civilians in Novaci should be protected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: -- interrupting you, Mr. Nobilo. General Blaskic, I have some questions here. Could you throw some light on this? What was the process used for numbering your orders? Was it descending order, ascending order? I don't know if I've understood correctly, but your order 312 is before your order 310, and ordinarily, the 310 would come before the 312. I don't know if I've understood you correctly. In any case, I would like to know how the numbering of the orders was done.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first number, "01," meant that the order was being issued by me, number "4" is the number of the month, and number "312" is the number under which it is registered. The moment the order reaches the typist who keeps that record book, she enters it under the first available number in the register, but at the time, this job was being done by one of the five, six, or seven officers who were in the command. I personally did not make any entries, and the typist still had not arrived, whose duty it would have normally been. It was rather confusing, the whole situation, and there may have been some errors made, but the rule was to fill in the first available space in the register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, General, the war diary, would you enter the time a document is being sent, or the time when it is being registered?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In most cases, when the document is being drafted, it is entered into the operative logbook. When it will be delivered, that is left for a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me draw your attention to 13.20. It says: "Approach test, addressed to the British Battalion, 01-4," et cetera. What does that mean? What happened at 13.20? Was that document written then, or was it sent at that time, in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I assume that that was the time when the document was sent.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it possible then that if the document was sent to the British Battalion at 13.20, that it may have been drafted before the document at 13.10, 01-4-312?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it could have been drafted before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue. We have another three minutes left. If I remember correctly, we had reached 13.30 hours, your warning to Cerkez that in the village of Novaci, where the front line was being broken through, that he should take care of civilians.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At 13.31, the artillery commander informed us that target 1 had been fired at. At 13.37, we again received a report from the Military Intelligence Service that a group of the BH army forces had been surrounded in town, without ammunition, and the UN is requesting their pulling out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "in town," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I mean the territory of Vitez municipality. At 13.38, I again addressed the artillery command to fire at target 1, giving them the same elements. At 13.40, I was informed, by the Military Intelligence Service, that the situation was bad at Kuber, and that the Muslim armed forces were active there, and that they were carrying out massacres at Kuber.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps this would be a convenient time to break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. In order to avoid interrupting you too often, General Blaskic, when you resume with the chronology minute by minute, of course, I understand it's your way of testifying, but if you might try to work in such a way that the Judges don't have some information, the contents of some information. What I was struck by is that often your counsel says you don't know the contents of the document. You say, "No. That's correct, I don't." Well, if nobody knows the contents, if you don't, if the Defence counsel doesn't, I don't know what the Prosecution is going to do, and that causes a bit of a problem to us. In the second point, I was speaking about methodology here, this would help us: Sometimes you say, "I asked for such a such information," and then we don't know whether there was an answer, or whether anything happened afterwards. If something is important to you, of course, I understand. Not everything is always important, and you're the only one that can know that, and we will evaluate that later on, but do not try to leave us drifting, because sometimes you say, "13.30, I asked for this, in this amount of time," but I'm not sure after that the answer is going to follow, or the contents of a document. If a document has been definitively lost, it's not going to be very useful to know that you numbered it, because we don't know anything about it. Those are a few comments I wanted to make, only in order to facilitate the proper conduct of the trial. I think we can stop now, it's 6.00. Rest up, and we'll try to rest as well. The registrar, we begin tomorrow at 10.00; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 6.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 9th day of March, 1999, at 10.00 a.m.
